title: Getting Secrets into Kubernetes: External Secrets Operator
intro: The secret lives in Vault (or AWS Secrets Manager, or Google Secret Manager). The pod needs it as an environment variable or a file. The External Secrets Operator bridges the two: an ExternalSecret object says 'copy this path into that Kubernetes Secret, and keep it in sync'. You're working in namespace shop.

steps.prompt: Check the connections to secret stores that the operator knows about, both namespaced and cluster-wide.
steps.fake_output:
NAMESPACE   NAME                                          AGE   STATUS   CAPABILITIES   READY
            clustersecretstore.external-secrets.io/vault   90d   Valid    ReadWrite      True
steps.explanation: One cluster-wide store, pointing at Vault, and it's valid.
steps.why: A SecretStore holds how to reach and authenticate to the backend, here Vault's Kubernetes auth: the operator presents its service account token and Vault checks it with the cluster. So the cluster holds no Vault password. If this shows Ready False, no secret anywhere syncs, and that's the first place to look.

steps.prompt: List the ExternalSecrets in namespace shop and whether each has synced.
steps.fake_output:
NAME          STORE   REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS              READY
shop-db       vault   1h                 SecretSynced        True
shop-stripe   vault   1h                 SecretSyncedError   False
steps.explanation: shop-db is in sync. shop-stripe is failing.
steps.why: The operator re-reads the source every refresh interval and updates the Kubernetes Secret if it changed. A failing ExternalSecret doesn't delete the existing Secret, so pods keep running on the last good value, and the failure is silent until that value is rotated at the source.

steps.prompt: Find out why shop-stripe isn't syncing.
steps.fake_output:
Spec:
  Data:
    Remote Ref:
      Key:       shop/stripe
      Property:  api_key
    Secret Key:  STRIPE_API_KEY
Status:
  Conditions:
    Message:  could not get secret data from provider
    Reason:   SecretSyncedError
Events:
  Warning  UpdateFailed  2m  external-secrets  Error making API request. URL: GET https://vault.internal/v1/secret/data/shop/stripe  Code: 403. Errors: * permission denied
steps.explanation: Vault answered 403: the operator's Vault role isn't allowed to read secret/data/shop/stripe.
steps.why: 403 from Vault is a policy problem, not a missing secret (that would be 404). The fix is in Vault: add the path to the policy attached to the operator's role. Scope that policy per namespace or per team; a single operator identity that can read every secret in Vault makes the cluster as sensitive as Vault itself.

steps.prompt: The Vault policy has been fixed and the secret synced. Check the value that landed in the Kubernetes Secret shop-stripe, key STRIPE_API_KEY.
expected_commands: kubectl get secret shop-stripe -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.STRIPE_API_KEY}' | base64 -d
kubectl get secret shop-stripe -n shop -o jsonpath="{.data.STRIPE_API_KEY}" | base64 -d
kubectl get secret shop-stripe -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.STRIPE_API_KEY}' | base64 --decode
steps.hint: kubectl get secret shop-stripe -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.STRIPE_API_KEY}' | base64 -d
steps.explanation: The value from Vault, now in a normal Kubernetes Secret.
steps.why: That it took one command shows the limit of this approach: a Kubernetes Secret is base64, not encryption. Anyone with 'get secrets' in the namespace can read it. So restrict that permission tightly, turn on encryption at rest for etcd, and remember the alternatives that never create a Secret object: the Vault Agent injector or the Secrets Store CSI driver, which put the value in the pod's memory-backed filesystem only.

steps.prompt: The Secret has updated, but running pods read it into environment variables at start-up. Make the deployment shop in namespace shop pick up the new value.
expected_commands: kubectl rollout restart deployment shop -n shop
kubectl rollout restart deploy shop -n shop
steps.explanation: New pods start, one at a time, with the current secret.
steps.why: Environment variables are fixed when a container starts, so a changed Secret reaches nobody until the pods restart. Secrets mounted as files do update in place after a minute or so, but only help if the app re-reads the file. Tools such as Reloader restart deployments automatically when their Secrets change. Until one of those is in place, 'we rotated the secret' and 'the app is using the new secret' are different statements (identity-incident-003).
